name: Kriang
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Gehrmann, Ryan. 2017. The historical phonology of Kriang, a Katuic language. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society 10(1): 114-139. hdl:10524/52402 (CC-BY; University of Hawai'i Press). Supporting: Smith, Ronald L. 1973. Reduplication in Ngeq. Mon-Khmer Studies 4: 85-111.
catalog_locator: Gehrmann 2017 sec. 2 'Phonological description', p. 117, second paragraph after the section heading through the first epenthesis sentence. Supporting: Smith 1973 sec. 1.2 'Intonation', p. 88.
catalog_quote: [Gehrmann 2017:117] The canonical Kriang word may be monosyllabic or disyllabic. In disyllabic words, the second syllable, or the main syllable, is stressed and equivalent in its phonotactics to monosyllables. The unstressed first syllable of a disyllabic word, or the presyllable, is deficient in comparison to the main syllable in that its inventory of permissible initial and final consonants is severely limited and in that it does not carry a phonemic vowel. The Kriang phonological word shape may be summarized as follows: (P1(P2)).C1(C2)V(ː)(F) A presyllable must contain a P1 onset but a P2 coda is not required. If no P2 coda is present, an epenthetic central vowel [ɐ] is inserted between P1 and the main syllable onset C1. [Smith 1973:88] In a reduplicated couplet the last syllable of the couplet receives the greatest stress of the word and has the highest intonation of the clause or sentence. The first word or syllable of the couplet is usually on a level tone like the rest of the clause or sentence; the last syllable receives greater stress, higher intonation and longer duration.
world_status: statement found in an open source

Sec. 2.2 (p. 104) 'The noun reduplications in Ngeq do not change the int…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In Ngeq's two-syllable reduplicated descriptive couplets the last syllable carries the greatest stress of the word, together with the highest pitch and longest duration; the first syllable is level like the rest of the clause. This is consistent with the Katuic iambic word template (Gehrmann 2018: 133, main/final syllable always prominent, presyllable always unstressed; Kriang listed in Table 5) and with Chia 2014: 13 (pre-syllables 'typically unstressed'), so word stress falls on the final (main) syllable; no source gives a dedicated stress rule for ordinary non-reduplicated Ngeq words.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Smith's statement is restricted to reduplicated adverbial-descriptive couplets and is framed as intonation; he adds (p. 104) that noun reduplications do not change sentence intonation. Chia 2014's 'typically unstressed' for pre-syllables is hedged and cited from Alves 2006 rather than argued for Ngeq.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (the 'stress of the word') for disyllabic descriptive couplets, but tied to clause/sentence intonation (the couplet is the intonation peak of the clause); the Katuic-general statements concern the maximally disyllabic prosodic word. No citation-form or instrumental data.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern the same language ngeq1245 [ngt]: Smith 1973 'Ngeq' (Se Kong river, Saravane province; treats Ngeq, Ngkriang and Khiang as dialects of one language); Chia 2014 'Ngeq (also known as Kriang)' with speakers from villages near Pakse, Champasak; Gehrmann 2017/2018 'Kriang' (Sekong province; dialects Kriang Kaleum and Kriang Tha Taeng). Smith's stress statement is about reduplicated descriptive couplets, not a general word-stress rule.

In disyllabic words, the second syllable, or the main syllable, is stressed and equivalent in its phonotactics to monosyllables. new_statements.rule_in_words: Kriang words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables (presyllable + main syllable); stress always falls on the main syllable, which is word-final; the presyllable is unstressed with a predictable epenthetic [ɐ]. Hence word stress is fixed on the final syllable of the phonological word.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for stress. The author notes presyllables with other initials occur mainly in expressives, Lao loans (e.g. /mɐlɛŋ/ 'cancer') and reduplications, but says nothing about their stress; words longer than two syllables are not discussed.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (mono- or disyllabic citation forms). Description explicitly 'accounts for both KK and KTT' dialects, with examples mainly from Kriang Tha Taeng; Klor (=Khlor) is a Kriang dialect per ISO CR 2018-008 by the same author but is not separately described.
new_statements.identity_note: khlo1239 'Khlor' [llo] is a retired code: ISO 639-3 CR 2018-008 (Gehrmann) retired it as a duplicate of Kriang [ngt] — Klor [klɔːr] is a Kriang dialect spoken only in Ko' village, Sekong province, 'completely mutually intelligible with Kriang'. Glottolog now has the language-level node ngeq1245 'Kriang-Khlor', which is a separate target in our source list (scan classification the named source could not be reached naming this same Gehrmann 2017 paper; no files held there). The quoted statement describes Kriang as a whole (both Kriang Kaleum and Kriang Tha Taeng dialects, examples mainly KTT), not Klor specifically. Recommend cataloguing under ngeq1245 and treating khlo1239 as an alias; the files saved here serve both keys.

The l…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (rule 01 = unstressed presyllable + stressed main syllable) and as Gehrmann 2017 p.117; adds the detail that the unstressed presyllable's vowel assimilates to the stressed vowel (a phonetic correlate of the stress asymmetry). Independent 1971 evidence from a Kriang speaker, so it also corroborates the existing statement. Open-copy access needed automated download -k (sealang.net serves a self-signed expired certificate; port 80 refused) since the the Internet Archive holds the landing page but not the per-page DjVu files.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are monosyllables or presyllable + main syllable; the presyllable is unstressed and the main (second = final) syllable carries the stress. Huffman states this only in passing, as the premise of a vowel-assimilation note: the schwa of the unstressed presyllable tends to copy the vowel of the stressed syllable. No statement about words longer than two syllables; the notebook's word lists and the 42-spread vocabulary notebook (informant note, word list, grammar sentences) contain no other prosodic remark and no stress marks.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; the presyllable-vowel assimilation is called a 'tendency', not a rule
new_statements.identity_note: Huffman's informant note (Notebook 6, p.1): "Ngeh /ŋɛʔ/ (means 'no') Ngeh is a general term for several dialects, including Kriang, Ta'Oi, Kantu, Trao. Mr. Boun Xou Leuangvilay is a speaker of Kriang, which is mutually comprehensible with TaOi, but not with Kantu or Trao. He can understand a speaker of Katang, also a Ngeʔ language. Professor of Natural Sciences at Collège de Saravane, Pakse. Comes from Ban Baak, Tasseng Ta'oi (taa 'ooiʔ), Meuang Ta'Oi, Saravane Province. Says these five languages can all be referred to as Bru!" Notebook 18's CONSONANTS page (scan p.31) also calls the language "Kriang". So the data are Kriang of Ban Baak; the notebooks do not say whether this is the Klor/Khlor variety that khlo1239 (retired ISO llo) names, and our check folder's header records that Gehrmann's ISO change request 2018-008 treats Khlor as a dialect of Kriang [ngt]. A second Huffman "Analysis of Ngeh" notebook (24a, 1979, informant Chinda, Thailand) exists in the same archive and was not opened (not a listed work).

tone.quote: I have not heard any pre-gottalised final nasals in the speech of my Chatong and Ta Oi' informants. In fact, a high-rising-falling pitch always accompanies the post-glottalisation in Ta Oi' and Chatong. I suspect that both pre- and post-glottalisation are perhaps part of the process of 'a non-tonal language becoming tonal'.
